GK-13.c01: If you crash but are not badly hurt, act to prevent more damage and injuries.
The **5 basic steps** at any accident → protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured, collect the required information, report the accident.
Think in time order → make the scene safe, get help coming, help people, then do the paperwork.
GK-13.c02: Your **first job** at any crash is to stop a second accident from happening at the same spot.
Your truck is involved → move it to the **side of the road**, so it prevents another crash and keeps traffic moving.
Stopping to help → park **away from** the wreck, because emergency vehicles need that space.
Turn on your **4-way flashers** and place reflective triangles so other drivers see them in time.
GK-13.c03: Have a cell phone or CB → call for help **before you get out** of your truck.
No phone or radio → first **protect the scene**, then phone the police or send someone to phone.
Figure out **exactly where you are** so you can give the precise location.
GK-13.c04: If someone **trained** (like a medic) is already treating people, let them work and help only if asked.
Do not move a badly injured person unless there is danger from **fire or passing traffic**; moving them can worsen injuries.
Control heavy bleeding with **direct pressure** on the wound, and keep hurt people **warm**.
GK-13.c05: If you were in the accident, you must file an **accident report** and collect the information for it.
Get each driver's name, address, and **DL number**, plus plate numbers and types of vehicles, and the owner's name and address if not the driver.
Record the officer's **name, badge number, and agency**, plus names and addresses of injured people and witnesses.
Note the damage, the **exact location**, and each vehicle's direction of travel.
[CA] The SR 1 report to DMV is due **within 10 days** if there is injury, death, or damage over **$1,000**.
GK-13.c06: Truck fires come from five sources → after accidents, **tires**, the electrical system, fuel, and cargo.
Prevent fires with pre-trip and en route inspections, safe procedures, and a **charged extinguisher**.
Untrained drivers have turned small fires into **bigger ones**, so learn how your extinguisher works before you need it.
GK-13.c07: After accidents → **spilled fuel** and improper use of flares; electrical → short circuits from damaged insulation and loose connections.
Tire fires come from **under-inflated tires** and **dual tires that touch**, which build heat through friction and flexing.
Fuel → driver smoking, improper fueling, loose fuel connections; cargo → flammable cargo, cargo not properly sealed or loaded, **poor ventilation**.
GK-13.c08: Pre-trip, fully inspect the **electrical, fuel, and exhaust systems**, tires, and cargo, and make sure the extinguisher is **charged**.
At **every stop** on a trip, check the tires, wheels, and truck body for any **sign of heat**.
Check gauges often for overheating, use mirrors to look for **smoke**, and be careful with anything flammable.
GK-13.c09: Stop in an **open spot** away from buildings, trees, brush, and vehicles; **never pull into a service station**, which is full of fuel.
Engine fire → shut the engine off and **avoid opening the hood**; van or box cargo fire → keep the **doors shut** so the fire gets no oxygen.
Stay as far away as possible, **upwind**, aim at the **base** of the fire, and keep going until the burning material has cooled.
**B:C** extinguisher → electrical fires and burning liquids; **A:B:C** adds wood, paper, and cloth.
**Never use water** on electrical fires (shock) or gasoline fires (spreads); unsure which extinguisher, especially with HazMat → wait for firefighters.
GK-13.c10: Never drink on duty, and drink **no alcohol at all** within **4 hours** before going on duty.
[CA] It is illegal to drive a CMV with a BAC of **0.04% or more**; below 0.04% is still not automatically safe or legal.
The liver processes only about **1/3 ounce of alcohol per hour**, so coffee or cold showers do nothing; **only time** lowers your BAC.
**One drink** = 12 oz 5% beer = 5 oz 12% wine = **1½ oz** 80-proof liquor; BAC depends on how much, how fast, and your weight.
Alcohol first hits **judgment and self-control**, so drinkers cannot tell they are getting drunk.
GK-13.c11: It is illegal to be under the influence of any **controlled substance**, amphetamines ("pep pills," "uppers," "bennies"), narcotics, or anything making you unsafe.
Prescription and OTC drugs, like **cold medicines**, can cause drowsiness; a doctor's drug is OK only if the doctor says it won't affect safe driving.
Never take a drug to hide tiredness; **rest** is the only cure for fatigue.
**Alcohol makes other drugs much stronger**, so the safest rule is not to mix drugs and driving at all.
GK-13.c12: If you are **too sick to drive safely**, do not drive.
In an emergency, drive only as far as the **closest place where it is safe to stop**.
GK-13.c13: Every CMV driver must be able to **spot hazardous cargo** and know whether they can haul it without an **"H" endorsement**.
Anyone applying for an original or renewal "H" must pass a **TSA security threat assessment**, a federal background check.
You start it **after** applying for your CDL, passing all knowledge tests, and turning in a valid medical form.
Give a TSA agent your **fingerprints, a fee**, a copy of your CLP, and one ID.
GK-13.c14: **HazMat** is anything that could harm people's health or safety, or damage property, while being shipped.
There are **9 numbered hazard classes**, e.g. 1 explosives, 2 gases, 3 flammable liquids like gasoline, 7 radioactive, 8 corrosives.
**ORM-D** (like hair spray) and **combustible liquids** (like fuel oils) have no class number.
GK-13.c15: HazMat rules have **3 goals** → contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
Shippers warn of risk with a **shipping paper** and **diamond-shaped labels**, since you may be hurt and unable to speak after a crash.
HazMat papers must be marked or kept **on top**, in a door pouch or in clear view within reach, and on the **driver's seat** when you leave.
GK-13.c16: Placards are outside warning signs showing the hazard class; you need **at least 4 identical** ones, front, rear, and both sides.
Each placard is at least **9.84 inches (250 mm) square**, set on a point as a diamond; answer this, not 10¾ inches, on the test.
ID numbers are **4 digits** after "UN" or "NA," listed in the DOT **Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)**.
Placards required → you need an **"H" endorsement**; not required → you may drive without one; driving placarded without an H is a crime.
Tank endorsement → each tank over **119 gallons** and **1,000 gallons or more** total; on the test, tank only → N, tank with placarded HazMat → X.
